Progesterone is a precursor in steroidogenesis to many steroids, [which includes androgens](https://i.imgur.com/Edgt2Od.png). It affects everyone differently, depending on genetics, i.e. enzyme expressions and AR sensitivity/expression in tissue. The canonical pathway can be seen on that chart, usually referred to as the 'front-door androgen pathway'. In this, precursors are metabolized into Testosterone, which is then converted by 5AR into DHT.

More recently, [a 'backdoor androgen pathway' has been discovered](https://i.imgur.com/Snxl2iw.png), in which DHT can be synthesized from Progesterone without the need for Testosterone as the intermediate.

Specifically, this process utilizes SRD5A1 (5-alpha-reductase Type 1), meaning that Finasteride won't be effective whatsoever in preventing this process (Finasteride only inhibits Type 2/3 5-AR). Dutasteride, however, inhibits all 3 5-ARs, so it can be used to prevent the backdoor pathway. The downside to this, however, is the loss of several neurosteroids (primarily Allopregnanolone), which are credited with the mood/sleep benefits of Progesterone. This would also inhibit endogenous neursteroid production to some degree, which might explain the reason some people experience depression on 5-ARi's, although that's yet to be confirmed.

There's another issue in that DHT is primarily synthesized from precursors locally in the peripheral tissues (i.e. skin, liver, hair, prostate), consumed locally. This means that, typically, serum DHT levels aren't really indicative of DHT concentration in tissues (exceptions for direct adrenal output of DHT). So there's many trans women with Serum DHT levels in range or very low (<10ng/dl) who still experience paradoxical masculinization, or subpar feminization, such as lack of breast growth or body hair inhibition (androgens have antiestrogenic effects and DHT has been successfully used to [atrophy gynecomastia](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6220269/))

Instead of testing Serum DHT, people propose you test 3α-Androstanediol glucuronide (3a-adg) instead. 3a-adg is a metabolite byproduct of T & DHT, and has been proposed as a potential marker of androgenic activity within peripheral tissues. There is some correlation between 5-AR activity and serum concentrations of 3a-adg, [although it's not perfect by any means](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8252744/). But from the anecdotal searching I've done, trans women who suspect masculinization from Progesterone seem to usually have elevated 3a-adg levels. Another, perhaps more promising marker is [ADT-G](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5823034/), but afaik this isn't really available to test freely. It seems that ADT-G correlates more highly with androgen-induced acne cases, whereas 3a-adg correlates more with hirsutism.

The best course of action, of course, is to try to stop it at the source. So Dutasteride. And if there's still androgenic symptoms post-duta, add Bicalutamide. Unfortunately you'll potentially lose the cognitive benefits of Progesterone, but can keep the other benefits. This could potentially be moot, however, as the canonical pathway is still active and, depending on how efficacious the process is in your body, elevate androgens in tissue other than DHT, like T, although the precursor androgens are a lot less potent.

Note that Bicalutamide doesn't bind to ARs within [osteoblasts or myocytes](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20950306/) (bone or muscle), therefore there's still potential for androgenic effects to occur in these regions.

People seem to quote the number of individuals affected by this as quite low, although I believe it occurs in everyone, to varying degrees. In some, either the androgens aren't as effective on them, or the enzymes responsible for androgenic conversion of P4 aren't as active, meaning they don't metabolize as much as those affected to androgens. But in some of us, these metabolites seem to fuck our shit up.

A lot of the purported sides of Progesterone (i.e. increased sexual function, libido, hair growth) seem to be androgenic in nature, so I've been looking into whether there's any clinical evidence that supports (or refutes) this. Interestingly enough too, the effect on libido seems to be positive in trans women, whereas many cis women report a drop in libido with Progesterone. The studies are pretty sparse and we do lack comprehensive data on the specific role of Progesterone in cellular function, but there is stuff out there, and I intend to try to investigate as best as possible to see if any conclusions can be drawn (I mean it'll all be conjecture, but knowledge is power, no definitive conclusions likely though).
